description:
We’re a multi-skilled team passionate about building an interactive asteroid impact simulator using NASA data. 
Our strengths:  AI/ML,  web/app dev,  design & storytelling,  pitching.
We’re looking for space science enthusiasts, data explorers, and creative visualizers to join us in making planetary defense exciting and impactful!
summary:
We developed FireSync, a full-stack spatial web platform and Incident Harmonisation Grid.

Currently, NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellites track active fires using mismatched resolutions (1km vs. 375m) and varying flyover schedules. This creates overlapping, confusing data for emergency response teams. FireSync addresses this by acting as a universal data translator. It ingests raw satellite telemetry and applies the HDBSCAN density-based clustering algorithm to automatically clean the noise, prevent double-counting, and merge overlapping pixels into unified "Active Fire Complexes" on an interactive map.

It transforms chaotic satellite noise into actionable intelligence. Disaster management teams gain a de-duplicated, tactical dashboard showing true fire boundaries and cumulative intensity (in Megawatts) for rapid, life-saving resource deployment. Simultaneously, climate researchers and forest departments can instantly export these harmonised datasets for predictive climate modelling, completely bypassing weeks of manual data engineering.
details:
FireSync is a spatial web platform that ingests raw, mismatched NASA satellite telemetry (1km MODIS and 375m VIIRS). It uses the HDBSCAN spatial clustering algorithm to automatically clean false alarms, prevent double-counting, and merge overlapping pixels into unified "Active Fire Complexes" on a single interactive map.

It transforms chaotic satellite noise into actionable intelligence. For disaster management teams (like the NDRF or fire chiefs), it provides a de-duplicated tactical map showing true fire boundaries and cumulative energy (in Megawatts) for faster, life-saving resource allocation. For climate researchers, it allows instant export of harmonised data for predictive modelling, saving weeks of manual data engineering.

Tools & Tech Stack:

  • Frontend: Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Scikit-learn (HDBSCAN algorithm)
  • Database: Supabase (PostgreSQL with the PostGIS spatial extension)
  • Deployment: GitHub, Vercel , Render

Instead of basic overlay mapping or standard K-Means clustering (which requires a user to guess the number of fires beforehand), we creatively applied density-based spatial clustering. This allows the system to autonomously find the true perimeters of fires while aggressively dropping false thermal anomalies (like sun glints off lakes) as noise, completely removing human guesswork.

We prioritised execution speed, modularity, and tactical usability. Knowing emergency responders operate in high-stress environments, we factored in the need for a clutter-free, dark-mode UI to reduce eye strain. Technically, we considered the risk of browser crashes from massive global datasets, solving this by offloading heavy spatial filtering directly to the PostGIS database index rather than the backend memory.
